text: Mark's Gospel employs an intercalation technique in the story of Jairus's daughter and the woman with the haemorrhage (Mark 5:21–43), sandwiching one narrative within another to create a mutual commentary between the two episodes. Both figures approach Jesus in desperation, both involve the number twelve, and the delay caused by the woman raises the dramatic stakes for the dying girl.

The chiasm in Matthew 7:6 structures the passage around the central prohibition against giving what is holy to dogs. The A-B-B'-A' pattern frames the warning within the broader context of judgement and discernment, inviting the reader to reflect on the relationship between the outer and inner elements.

The parable of the Prodigal Son follows the standard rabbinic mashal form, opening with a brief narrative premise, developing through a three-part structure of departure, degradation, and return, and closing with a rhetorical turn that subverts the expected resolution. The elder brother's resentment at the end destabilises any simple reading.

Jesus's words in the Nazareth synagogue sermon in Luke 4:18–19 echo Isaiah 61:1–2, but the citation strategically omits the phrase 'and the day of vengeance of our God,' transforming the prophetic oracle from a message of judgement and restoration into a unilateral declaration of liberation. The omission is a deliberate hermeneutical move.

The audience would have understood the reference to the Good Samaritan as a deliberate provocation. Luke's narrative skillfully exploits the ethnic animosity between Jews and Samaritans to invert the expected hierarchy of piety, making the despised outsider the exemplar of covenant faithfulness.

This pericope follows the typical miracle-story form identified by form critics: a description of the illness's severity, an expression of desperation by the supplicant, the thaumaturge's authoritative word or gesture, an immediate demonstration of healing, and an acclamation by the crowd. The pattern serves to establish Jesus's authority within a recognisable narrative convention.

The Fourth Gospel's prologue (John 1:1–18) exhibits a chiastic structure that moves from the Word's pre-existence with God, to his rejection by the world, to the incarnation as the climactic centre, and back outward to the revelation of the Father. The careful architecture signals that the prologue functions as a hermeneutical lens for the entire Gospel.

Mark's use of the 'messianic secret' functions as a literary device that controls the narrative's pace and intensifies the reader's anticipation. Jesus repeatedly commands silence after healings and exorcisms, yet the commands are consistently broken, creating a dramatic irony in which the reader knows what the characters within the story fail to grasp fully.

The Beatitudes in Matthew 5:3–12 are carefully arranged in two stanzas of four, with the ninth beatitude functioning as an expansion. The first four address the dispossessed in passive constructions, while the second four describe active virtues. This poetic architecture suggests deliberate literary shaping beyond mere sayings collection.

Paul's argument in Romans 9–11 employs the rhetorical device of diatribe, using an imaginary interlocutor to raise objections that Paul then answers. The questions 'What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part?' (9:14) and 'You will say to me then, Why does he still find fault?' (9:19) are not genuine dialogues but literary foils that advance Paul's theological argument.

The narrative frame of the Book of Job provides an interpretive key for the poetic dialogues within. The prose prologue establishes Job's righteousness and the heavenly wager, while the epilogue resolves the tension, but the central poetry refuses easy resolution. This generic hybridity is a deliberate literary strategy.

The use of inclusio in the Gospel of Mark, where the tearing of the heavens at Jesus's baptism (1:10) finds its counterpart in the tearing of the Temple veil at his death (15:38), creates a symbolic frame around the entire narrative. Both moments involve a divine disclosure and a rupture of boundaries.

The repeated phrase 'and immediately' in Mark's Gospel is not merely a stylistic tic but a narrative device that generates urgency and momentum. Occurring over forty times, it propels the reader through Jesus's ministry at a breathless pace, reinforcing the eschatological urgency of his proclamation.

The episode of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) interrupts the narrative flow of the Festival of Tabernacles discourse and is widely regarded as a later interpolation. Its placement, however, creates a thematic resonance with the surrounding material on judgement and testimony, suggesting a redactor's literary sensitivity.

The rhetorical structure of 1 Corinthians 13 follows a tripartite pattern common in Greco-Roman encomia: the indispensability of love (vv. 1–3), the description of love's attributes (vv. 4–7), and the permanence of love contrasted with the transience of spiritual gifts (vv. 8–13). Each section builds cumulatively toward the climactic assertion of love's supremacy.

The temptation narrative in Matthew 4:1–11 is structured around three quotations from Deuteronomy, each introduced by Jesus with the formula 'It is written.' The progression from physical appetite to religious spectacle to political power follows a carefully graded intensification, with each temptation probing a deeper dimension of messianic identity.

The author of Hebrews employs an intricate pattern of exposition and exhortation, alternating between theological argument and paraenetic application. The shifts in genre signal to the reader that doctrinal exposition always serves a pastoral purpose, preventing the theological sections from becoming abstract speculation.

The Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55) is densely woven with allusions to the Song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10), the Psalms, and prophetic oracles. Mary's song functions on one level as personal thanksgiving and on another as a programmatic announcement of the social reversal that Luke's Gospel will narrate, making it a microcosm of Lukan theology.
Jesus was born in Bethlehem during the reign of Herod the Great. The Gospel of Luke describes the journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem as necessitated by a census ordered by Caesar Augustus.

Archaeological excavations at Capernaum have uncovered the remains of a first-century house that was later enclosed within a fourth-century octagonal church structure. The site is traditionally identified as Peter's house.

The doctrine of the Trinity holds that God exists as three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — in one divine essence. This formulation was developed through the ecumenical councils of the fourth century.
The Synoptic Gospels are Matthew, Mark, and Luke. They are called synoptic because they can be viewed together in parallel columns, and they share substantial material in common.

The city of Jerusalem sits at an elevation of approximately 754 metres above sea level in the Judaean mountains. The city was the political and religious centre of Jewish life during the Second Temple period.
The apostle Peter, originally named Simon, was a fisherman from Bethsaida before becoming a disciple of Jesus. According to church tradition, he was martyred in Rome under Emperor Nero.
The Greek word logos appears in the prologue of John's Gospel and is typically translated as Word. The term carried rich connotations in both Jewish wisdom literature and Greek philosophy.
The Second Temple was extensively renovated and expanded by Herod the Great beginning around 20 BCE. The project employed thousands of labourers and took decades to complete.

The four canonical Gospels were accepted as authoritative by the early church by the end of the second century. Irenaeus of Lyons argued that there must be exactly four Gospels, corresponding to the four winds and the four living creatures of Revelation.
Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate, the Roman prefect of Judea. Crucifixion was a common form of capital punishment in the Roman Empire, reserved primarily for slaves and insurrectionists.

The resurrection of Jesus is the central claim of Christian faith. According to the New Testament, he appeared to his disciples on multiple occasions over a period of forty days before ascending to heaven.

The Gospel of Mark records that Jesus taught in parables, and when he was alone with his disciples he explained everything to them privately. Many of these parables use agricultural imagery drawn from everyday life in Galilee.
